title: Japan Declares Cybersecurity Emergency, Experts Nod to AI
source_used: PCMag (read first on the PCMag Middle East copy, then confirmed on the US page); relays The Financial Times and Reuters
key_facts: PCMag says Japan has declared a cybersecurity emergency after a spate of attacks on its companies in recent weeks, and that some experts point to AI.

According to The Financial Times, over 20 major firms, including the convenience-store chain Lawson and the car-rental operator Times Car, have reported attacks, with tens of millions of pieces of customer data lost, among them 1.67 million customer email addresses from the booking system of rail operator JR East.

Cybersecurity minister Toshiharu Furukawa called the situation 'extremely critical' and Masaaki Taira, head of the National Cybersecurity Strategy Headquarters, called it an 'emergency in cyberspace'.

Masaki Hiraoka of Blackpanda told the FT that even if the attacks have not been explicitly linked to AI, the technology lets hackers do what once needed time-consuming preparation, so smaller services could become viable targets.
Nobuo Miwa of S&J Corp told Reuters the attacks resemble 'carpet bombing' and that AI tools may help foreign hackers overcome language barriers.
Data from TrendAI shared with Reuters show Japan recorded more cybersecurity incidents in the first nine months of 2026 than in all of last year.
The Financial Services Agency has reportedly asked lenders to accept only identity documents with ID chips after driver's-licence images leaked in the Times Car attack.
quote_evidence: Japanese cybersecurity minister Toshiharu Furukawa said the situation was "extremely critical" at a meeting at the National Cybersecurity Strategy Headquarters.

Masaki Hiraoka ... told the FT that even if the recent spate of attacks hasn't been explicitly linked to AI use, the technology is enabling hackers to carry out attacks that once required time-consuming investigations ahead of time.
Japan recorded more cybersecurity incidents in the first nine months of 2026 than in all of last year, according to data from TrendAI shared with Reuters.
why_it_matters_hint: Customers of many Japanese firms have had personal data leaked, and officials treat the wave as an emergency while AI's role is suspected, not shown.
event_date: FT report and Japanese government meeting before 10 Oct 2026 (dates not stated); PCMag 10 Oct 2026 17:55 UTC, PCMag Middle East 11 Oct 2026
notes: The pool item is the PCMag Middle East copy, which adds a paragraph for Middle East businesses; the credited reporter is The Financial Times (with Reuters), relayed by PCMag. The FT and Reuters originals were not opened. Overlaps our 9 Oct 2026 Reuters entry on Korea and Japan hacks.
